stories.head: Former German spy chief Hanning arrested on treason suspicion
stories.stand: August Hanning, who ran Germany's BND foreign intelligence service until 2005, is accused of obtaining secret documents for a foreign agency.
body: German federal prosecutors have arrested August Hanning, a former head of the BND foreign intelligence service, on suspicion of treasonous espionage and attempted treason. He was detained on Tuesday at his home in Nordwalde, near Münster.

A former BND employee, identified only as Manfred D., was arrested in Bavaria. Prosecutors allege that from 2010 at the latest he passed Hanning internal BND material in return for payment, about 2,000 documents in all, many of them classified.

Prosecutors say Hanning used some of the material to draft analysis for a foreign intelligence officer and passed political information to that agency's representatives for years. The foreign service has not been named; reports say Russia is not involved.
Hanning led the BND for seven years until 2005. The current BND president, Martin Jaeger, said there could be no compromise on internal security. Both men are presumed innocent.

stories.head: Drones hit two ships off Bulgaria, one sinks with crew missing
stories.say: Drones have hit two merchant ships off Bulgaria. One, the Alfa Watan, sank and its crew are missing. All 18 crew of the other ship were rescued.
stories.stand: A Togo-flagged vessel sank and a grain carrier caught fire in Bulgaria's Black Sea economic zone, a day after a ship sank off Romania.
body: Sea and air drones struck two Turkish-owned merchant ships early on Tuesday about 70 nautical miles east of Byala, inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.

The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sank. A Bulgarian ferry found an overturned lifeboat and life jackets but none of its crew. The Palau-flagged Able, carrying wheat, caught fire; all 18 crew were taken off and two were treated in hospital in Varna.

Prime Minister Rumen Radev called the attack a blatant breach of international law but did not say who was responsible. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the developments very concerning.
The strikes came a day after a cargo ship sank off Romania, an attack Ukraine blamed on Russia.

stories.head: Yemen government claims Mocha and Taiz gains as Houthis target Aden airport
stories.say: In Yemen, government forces say they've retaken the port city of Mocha from the Houthis. Early on Wednesday, a Houthi missile landed near the runway at Aden airport.
stories.stand: Saudi-backed forces say they have retaken the port of Mocha and a Taiz peak; a Houthi missile landed near Aden's runway.
body: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces say they have recaptured the Red Sea port of Mocha, which the Houthis took in September, along with positions near the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Al Jazeera said it could not independently verify the battlefield claims.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said 100 fighter jets were supporting the ground offensive, which government forces call Operation Dawn of Yemen. On Wednesday they said they had tightened control of the highest peak in Taiz's Jabal Habashi district.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had stopped government attempts to advance towards Bab al-Mandeb.

Early on Wednesday, two ballistic missiles and several drones targeted Aden airport. One missile landed near the runway, and a Yemenia flight from Cairo was diverted to Jeddah. Yemen's transport ministry called it a serious escalation.

stories.head: Sudan army chief rules out talks as UN body demands ceasefire
stories.stand: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan said the army would fight until the RSF is driven out, as the UN Human Rights Council called for a truce.
body: Sudan's army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has rejected negotiations with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. Speaking in Merowe, northern Sudan, he said the army would pursue military victory until all territory was cleared.

His remarks came as the UN Human Rights Council voted 28 to 10, with 9 abstentions, to extend its fact-finding mission on Sudan. The resolution calls for an immediate and complete ceasefire without preconditions. Sudan had urged members to reject it.
The US has proposed a 90-day humanitarian ceasefire followed by talks. US adviser Massad Boulos recently met al-Burhan in Egypt.
The war began in April 2023. It has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced about 13 million.

stories.head: Trump approves firing squad execution for Fort Hood gunman
stories.say: President Trump has approved a firing squad execution for Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. It would be the first US military execution since 1961.
stories.stand: Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in 2009, faces the first US military execution since 1961.
body: President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in November 2009. More than 30 others were wounded.
The Pentagon announced the decision. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had recommended the execution, and the Army secretary will set the time and place.
A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in 2013. The US military has not carried out an execution since 1961.
Hasan can still challenge the sentence in federal civilian courts, which could delay it for years.

stories.head: Mexico arrests alleged Jalisco cartel fuel-theft boss 'El Tanque'
stories.stand: Iván Cazarín Molina, sanctioned by the US in 2024, was detained in Zapopan, Mexico's security minister said.
body: Mexican forces have arrested Iván Cazarín Molina, known as "El Tanque", in Zapopan in Jalisco state, Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch announced. The arrest took place on Monday 5 October.

Authorities describe him as a regional operator for the Jalisco New Generation Cartel in Veracruz, Oaxaca, Tabasco and Puebla. He is suspected of homicide, extortion, drug trafficking, money laundering and fuel theft.

The US Treasury sanctioned him in September 2024, saying his fuel-theft network earned tens of millions of dollars a year. He is also linked by authorities to a 2015 attack on an army helicopter. The allegations have not been tested in court.

stories.head: Myanmar leader visits Malaysia as returns pass 10,000
stories.stand: Min Aung Hlaing's two-day visit follows the repatriation of about 10,000 Myanmar nationals this year, drawing UN warnings.
body: Myanmar's leader Min Aung Hlaing is making a two-day visit to Malaysia on 7 and 8 October. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said repatriation of Myanmar nationals would be on the agenda.
About 10,000 people have been returned to Myanmar from Malaysia since January. Nearly 1,500 arrived by sea on Sunday.
The UN refugee agency said its staff were not allowed to check whether returnees chose freely. UN rights chief Volker Türk warned against forced returns to Myanmar.
Anwar said Myanmar must treat returnees fairly. Rights groups fear Rohingya refugees could be included. Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention.

stories.head: Seventh man arrested in RAF Fairford terror investigation
stories.say: A seventh man has been arrested in the RAF Fairford terror investigation. Police say the 22-year-old was held in Westminster on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
stories.stand: Counter-terrorism police held a 22-year-old British man in Westminster on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
body: Counter Terrorism Policing arrested a 22-year-old British national in the London borough of Westminster on 6 October. He is held on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, and properties in the area were searched.

He is the seventh person arrested in the inquiry. Five British men were arrested near the Gloucestershire airbase on 27 September, and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national on 1 October. Police say all six, men in their 20s, remain on bail.

The US has moved its bombers away from the base. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken of strong indications of Iranian involvement, ITV reports, while Iran has denied any part. Police describe it as a live investigation with several lines of enquiry.

stories.head: Officers who Tasered 92-year-old amputee in care home dismissed
stories.stand: A misconduct panel found two Sussex Police constables used excessive force on a wheelchair user with dementia in 2022.
body: Two Sussex Police officers have been dismissed without notice after a misconduct panel found them guilty of gross misconduct. PC Stephen Smith, 52, and PC Rachel Comotto, 37, have also been placed on the police barred list.

The case concerns a 92-year-old resident of a care home in St Leonards-on-Sea in June 2022. He used a wheelchair, had one leg amputated and had dementia. Officers were called after reports that he was holding a knife.

Within about a minute and a half of arriving, the officers used PAVA spray, a baton, a Taser and handcuffs. The panel, which sat from 28 September to 6 October, found the force excessive and unreasonable.

The man was taken to hospital, caught Covid-19 and died in July 2022. A pathologist found the officers' actions did not cause or contribute to his death. Both officers were cleared of assault at a criminal trial in May 2025.

stories.head: Student admits murdering woman at Tividale Airbnb
stories.stand: Benjamin Day, 20, changed his plea on the second day of his trial at Wolverhampton Crown Court.
body: Benjamin Day, 20, has admitted murdering a 24-year-old woman at an Airbnb property in Tividale, West Midlands, in December 2025. He changed his plea to guilty on 6 October, the second day of his trial.
The prosecution said Day, a University of Worcester forensics student from Redditch, had lined a room with plastic beforehand. The woman suffered 78 knife wounds.
Prosecutors said he began to dismember her body but stopped after cutting himself, then called 999. He was arrested in hospital. Day had been expected to argue self-defence.
He was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced on 4 December.

stories.head: Arson killer was freed after threatening petrol bomb, inquest hears
stories.stand: An inquest into a 2017 house fire that killed a mother and four children is examining Greater Manchester Police's earlier handling of threats.
body: An inquest at Bolton Coroner's Court is examining the deaths of a mother and four children after an arson attack on a house in Walkden in December 2017. It is expected to last about two months.

On 6 October, its second day, a Greater Manchester Police response officer gave evidence about an incident on 26 November 2017. Zak Bolland had damaged the house and sent a text threatening to petrol bomb it.

The inquest heard Bolland was released after a short 'no comment' interview, though he was on a suspended sentence. The officer said he was not aware of the threats or the suspended sentence at the time.
Bolland and David Worrall were later given life sentences with minimum terms of 40 and 37 years.

stories.head: 25 smuggling boats seized in air freight at East Midlands Airport
stories.stand: The National Crime Agency says it is the first time small-boat equipment has been found in air cargo.
body: The National Crime Agency (NCA) and Border Force seized 25 inflatable boats at East Midlands Airport on 2 October. The cargo was passing through the UK on its way from Turkey to the Netherlands.
Each boat is about nine metres long. Together they could carry around 1,700 people across the Channel, the agencies estimate.
Officials say it is the first such find in air freight. In July, 25 boats and 25 engines were seized at Felixstowe port.
The NCA says it has seized more than 1,600 boats and engines, which it believes is raising costs for smugglers. No arrests have been reported.

stories.head: Wales orders M4 road study and starts work on third Menai crossing
stories.stand: The Welsh Government set out plans for two congestion hotspots, including an 18-month study of road options around Newport.
body: The Welsh Government announced on 6 October an 18-month study of road-based options for the M4 around Newport. A preferred option will be chosen afterwards.

ITV reports the options could include junction closures and widening the Brynglas tunnels. Interim steps over five years include junction upgrades and new or improved stations at Cardiff Parkway, Magor and Undy.
Development work also begins on a third Menai crossing, covering design, environmental assessment and a business case. ITV puts the cost at about £670m and the timescale at eight to ten years.
Deputy Transport Minister Mark Hooper said measures aim to cut peak-hour traffic by up to around one in ten vehicles. Opposition parties said junction closures would only move congestion elsewhere.

stories.head: Badenoch to pitch tax cuts in closing Tory conference speech
stories.stand: The Conservative leader is set to frame the next election as a contest of ideas, backed by a youth national insurance cut.
body: Kemi Badenoch is due to close the Conservative conference in Birmingham with a speech centred on the economy, according to pre-briefed extracts. She is expected to call the next general election a battle of ideas over the nation's future.

The party has announced it would cut employer national insurance from 15% to 7.5% for workers aged 21 to 24. ITV reports a static cost of £3.25bn, with the party estimating a net cost of £2.3bn by 2029-30.
Badenoch says the national debt is above £2.9tn and argues growth must be a Conservative government's organising aim. The extracts also criticise Prime Minister Andy Burnham over public spending.
Labour called the national insurance plan unfunded. Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said his party would scrap the employer charge for all workers.

stories.head: Tories pledge £10bn 'Britannia Shield' air defence system
stories.stand: The Conservatives say a future government would build radar, command systems and interceptors to guard the UK against missiles and drones.
body: The Conservatives have pledged £10bn over ten years for an integrated air and missile defence system called Britannia Shield. It was announced at the party's Birmingham conference on 6 October.
The plan covers new radar, upgraded command and control, and more interceptor missiles with counter-drone capability. The party says a minimal working system would be ready within its first term.

A party press release first called it a British 'Iron Dome'. Kemi Badenoch later said it differed from Israel's system. The party says funding would come from its pledge to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting criticised the Conservatives' record on the armed forces. The Liberal Democrats said £10bn would not cover the whole UK.

stories.head: Greens face criticism after 'Zionism is racism' vote
stories.stand: European Greens and Kemi Badenoch condemned the motion, as most Green MPs also rejected it ahead of Thursday's by-election.
body: Green Party of England and Wales members voted 1,022 to 813 to define Zionism as a form of racism at their Brighton conference. The motion also backed a single Palestinian state in historic Palestine.
The European Green Party said it distanced itself from the motion and would seek clarity from the party's leadership. It restated its support for a two-state solution.
Four of the five Green MPs publicly rejected the motion. Leader Zack Polanski did not vote, having left to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, due on 8 October.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told ITV she was appalled by the vote. Polanski has said antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are distinct.

stories.head: Trump draws backlash for saying Iran could 'take out' LA
stories.stand: California leaders from both parties criticised the president's rally remarks; the White House says he was misunderstood.
body: At a midterm rally in Nebraska on Monday, Donald Trump said Iran could be allowed to take out Los Angeles and San Diego. He was speaking about the war with Iran and fuel prices.
California Governor Gavin Newsom called the remarks deranged and dangerous. He said state officials would monitor potential threats.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria also objected. Republican House candidate Jim Desmond said no American city was expendable.
The White House said Trump meant the US was fighting to stop Iran gaining the ability to strike such cities. Communications director Steven Cheung called the criticism a media overreaction.

stories.head: Separatist Parti Québécois wins Quebec election
stories.stand: The PQ will form a minority government, while the governing CAQ was reported to have lost all its seats.
body: The Parti Québécois won the most seats in Quebec's provincial election on 5 October. It fell short of the 64 seats needed for a majority in the 127-seat National Assembly.
Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon will become premier, ending eight years of Coalition Avenir Québec rule. The PQ won three seats in 2022.
He has promised a third independence referendum in his first term, but not before Donald Trump leaves office in January 2029. Polls put support for independence around 30%.
Prime Minister Mark Carney congratulated the PQ leader and offered co-operation on US tariffs, jobs and housing.

stories.head: AfD wins its first German state parliament speakership
stories.stand: Tobias Rausch was elected president of Saxony-Anhalt's parliament with support beyond his own party.
body: Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) was elected speaker of Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament on 6 October. He won 48 votes to 29 in the first round.
He is the first AfD politician to hold a state parliament presidency. The AfD won 43.8% in September's state election but has no majority.
The BSW party, with five seats, backed him in advance. The AfD and BSW together hold 44 seats, so some votes came from other groups in the secret ballot.

Rausch called himself pragmatic. He has faced cronyism allegations over staffing; he says he was not involved in the hiring decisions. The AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, seeks to become state premier in December.

stories.head: S&P 500 closes at another record as Treasury yields ease
stories.stand: Technology and energy-related shares led US stocks higher on Tuesday, with the S&P 500 finishing above 7,800 for a second day.
body: US stocks rose on Tuesday 6 October, with the S&P 500 setting a new closing record. The Dow and the Nasdaq also gained around half a percentage point.
Chip makers helped lead the advance. Marvell Technology rose 7–8% after raising its revenue targets linked to AI infrastructure, and AMD gained almost 3%.
Constellation Energy jumped after a long-term nuclear power deal with Google. Option Care Health soared on a takeover agreement.
The 10-year US Treasury yield slipped to about 5.27%, down from roughly 5.31%. Storage firms Seagate and Western Digital were among the biggest fallers.

stories.head: European shares rise for third day as bond yields retreat
stories.stand: Healthcare stocks led European markets higher on Tuesday, while London's FTSE 100 extended its recovery from a three-month low.
body: European stocks rose on Tuesday 6 October, the third straight day of gains. Eurozone government bond yields eased after touching multi-decade highs the previous week.
Healthcare shares led the market. Danish biotech Genmab rose more than 7% after a late-stage trial of a blood cancer drug combination it develops with AbbVie.
In London, the FTSE 100 gained about 0.4% to close near 10,542. Informa rose more than 5% after agreeing to buy events group Clarion.
Banks also advanced. Schneider Electric fell further after its large deal for PTC announced on Monday.

stories.head: CD&R and McKesson agree $5.8bn deal for Option Care Health
stories.stand: The US home infusion provider's shares jumped about a third after it agreed to a cash takeover by a private equity firm and drug distributor.
body: Option Care Health has agreed to be bought by private equity firm CD&R and drug distributor McKesson. The deal values the US company at about $5.8bn including debt.
Shareholders will receive $32.05 a share in cash. That is about 37% above Monday's closing price of $23.37.
CD&R will hold 51% and McKesson 49%, with McKesson investing about $1.4bn. McKesson has a possible route to buy CD&R's stake later, subject to conditions.
The companies expect the deal to close in the first half of 2027. It needs shareholder and regulatory approval. Option Care's shares rose about 33% on Tuesday.

stories.head: Informa to buy events group Clarion from Blackstone for £2.24bn
stories.stand: The FTSE 100 events and publishing group also plans to separate its Taylor & Francis academic publishing business.
body: Informa has agreed to buy Clarion Events from private equity firm Blackstone for £2.24bn. Clarion runs more than 100 business-to-business brands, including the ICE gaming show in Barcelona and the DSEI defence exhibition.
Informa plans to raise about £940m in new shares to help fund the purchase. It expects the deal to complete by the end of 2026.
The company also said it plans to separate Taylor & Francis, its academic publishing arm. It said fuller details would come with next year's results.
Blackstone bought Clarion in 2017 for £600m, according to trade outlet NEXT.io. Informa shares rose on the news.

stories.head: Google signs 20-year nuclear power deal with Constellation
stories.stand: Constellation will spend $4.3bn upgrading existing reactors to supply Google, sending its shares sharply higher on Tuesday.
body: Constellation Energy has signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Google. It covers 890 megawatts of new capacity from upgrades at existing nuclear reactors.
The work spans 11 Constellation-owned units in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. The company plans to invest $4.3bn, with the first upgrade expected by 2028.
A separate 15-year agreement covers about 2,700 megawatts from Constellation's existing plants. The firms also agreed a five-year cloud services deal.
Financial terms were not disclosed. Constellation shares rose more than 12% on Tuesday, and other power producers such as Vistra also gained.

stories.head: Putin approves UniCredit plan to sell most of its Russian bank
stories.stand: A presidential decree lets the Italian bank split its Russian unit and sell the retail and corporate business to a UAE-based investor.
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree allowing UniCredit to reorganise and sell part of its Russian subsidiary. Since 2022, such deals by banks from 'unfriendly' countries need presidential approval.
UniCredit will split the unit in two. It will keep a business handling international euro and dollar payments for clients not under sanctions.
The retail and corporate banking operations will go to an unnamed private investor based in the United Arab Emirates. No price has been published.
UniCredit expects the deal to complete in the first half of 2027. It still needs approval from Russia's central bank and Western regulators.

stories.head: German factory orders drop 10.6% in August
stories.stand: New orders fell far more than expected as large domestic contracts, including defence and transport equipment, unwound after a strong July.
body: Orders for German factories fell 10.6% in August from July, the Federal Statistics Office said. Economists had expected a drop of about 1%.
The fall was driven by fewer large domestic orders. Orders for military vehicles, aircraft, ships and trains dropped by more than 60%.
Excluding large orders, the level was almost unchanged from July. Over June to August, orders were 1.3% higher than in the previous three months.
July's increase was revised up to 3.2%. The economy ministry called August a marked setback but said public procurement makes orders highly volatile.

stories.head: US trade deficit widens to $105.6bn on record imports
stories.stand: The gap between US imports and exports grew 13.7% in August, more than economists expected, as goods imports rose sharply.
body: The US trade deficit in goods and services rose to $105.6bn in August, official data showed on Tuesday. That was up $12.7bn from a revised $92.8bn in July.
Imports climbed 4.3% to $420.8bn, while exports rose 1.4% to $315.2bn. Economists had forecast a deficit of about $102bn.
The Korea Times, citing economists, linked the import rise to strong consumer spending and business investment in equipment, including for AI.
For the year to date, the deficit is about 20% smaller than in the same period of 2025, the official release said.

stories.head: Physics Nobel goes to Francis Halzen for IceCube neutrino discovery
stories.say: This year's Nobel Prize in Physics goes to just one person, Francis Halzen. The 82-year-old is honoured for IceCube, which found high-energy neutrinos arriving from deep space.
stories.stand: The Belgian-born physicist is the sole winner, honoured for turning Antarctic ice into a detector for neutrinos arriving from deep space.
body: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics to Francis Halzen on Tuesday. He is a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and was born in Belgium.
The citation recognises his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. Halzen first proposed the detector in 1988.
IceCube uses about a cubic kilometre of ice at the South Pole fitted with light sensors. It records faint flashes made when neutrinos strike atomic nuclei in the ice.
The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor. Halzen, 82, said the award came as a great surprise. The prizes are presented on 10 December.

stories.head: Astronomers report a planet formed from a dying star's debris
stories.stand: A Warwick-led team says a gas giant orbiting a white dwarf appears to have formed after its star died, a first observational case.
body: Astronomers led by the University of Warwick report what they describe as the first evidence of a second-generation planet. Their study appeared in Nature Astronomy on 5 October.
The planet is a Jupiter-sized gas giant orbiting the white dwarf HS 0209+0832 about every 4.4 days. It was spotted using NASA's TESS satellite.
The white dwarf's atmosphere holds unusually high levels of zinc, copper and niobium. The team says this pattern points to elements made as the star died, from which the planet then formed.
The idea of such planets was proposed more than 15 years ago. The researchers told Science News that further study is needed to confirm the object's nature.

stories.head: Study suggests animals arose up to 200 million years before fossils show
stories.stand: A molecular clock analysis in Science Advances puts the origin of animals at 800 to 700 million years ago.
body: Researchers from the University of Oxford and Virginia Tech used a molecular clock to estimate when animals first appeared. The study was published in Science Advances on 2 October.
The method compares genetic differences among living organisms with estimated rates of change. It places the origin of animals between 800 and 700 million years ago.
The oldest accepted animal fossils date to about 574 million years ago. That would leave a gap of roughly 200 million years.
The authors say the analysis does not prove animals existed 800 million years ago. Body fossils from before the Ediacaran period have not been found.

stories.head: Engineer explains why an electrified pickle glows
stories.stand: A Portland State University researcher says sparks ignite hydrogen from electrolysis, while sodium gives the familiar orange light.
body: A Portland State University electrical engineer says he has explained a classic classroom demonstration. In it, a pickle wired to a mains socket glows orange.
He burnt more than 100 pickles in tests, according to the university. He concluded that electrolysis splits water and releases hydrogen gas.
Electrical sparks, not heat, then ignite that hydrogen, he says. Excited sodium ions from the brine produce the orange colour.
ScienceAlert reports the explanation combines two hypotheses that had competed. The work was presented at an Electrostatics Society of America meeting in June.

stories.head: Russia tells WHO no plague found after Irkutsk lab worker's death
stories.stand: The WHO says Russia reported no plague cases and contacts tested negative, though it has asked Moscow for more information.
body: The World Health Organization said on 6 October that Russia had reported no plague cases in the Irkutsk region. A laboratory worker there died earlier this month.
Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, attributes the death to pneumonia of unknown origin. It says the regional public health situation is stable.
About 200 contacts were placed under observation. CBS News reports that none tested positive for plague. The WHO says the risk to the public appears low.
The WHO has asked Russia for more details about the death. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also urged Moscow to share more information.

stories.head: Scientists watch signs of an early flu season led by H1N1
stories.stand: Nature reports early flu activity across the northern hemisphere, with a mutated H1N1 strain that antibodies recognise less well.
body: Flu activity is starting unusually early in parts of the northern hemisphere, Nature reports. It cites the UK, the US west coast and school outbreaks in Japan.
H1N1 made up 96% of fully subtyped US cases by 26 September, according to CDC data cited by Nature. H3N2 dominated last season.
Many recent H1N1 samples carry a mutation called G155E. A preprint led by Jesse Bloom found such viruses were neutralised less well by human blood samples.
The drop was most marked among teenagers and young adults. An Oxford epidemiologist told Nature an early start does not guarantee a severe season.

stories.head: Seven cancer types rising in under-50s in England, charity finds
stories.stand: World Cancer Research Fund analysis of NHS data shows bowel and womb cancer rates in younger adults more than doubled since 2001.
body: The World Cancer Research Fund analysed NHS England data for adults under 50. It compared 2001 with 2023.
Bowel cancer rose from 3.9 to 8.4 cases per 100,000. Womb cancer rose from 1.8 to 3.9 per 100,000 women, and prostate cancer from 1 to 3.6 per 100,000 men.
Kidney cancer cases roughly doubled, from 510 to 1,065. Breast, liver and pancreatic cancer rates also rose.
Cancer remains far more common in older people. NHS England urges people with persistent new symptoms to contact their GP. Cancer Research UK says some prostate rise may reflect overdiagnosis.

stories.head: Northern Ireland launches UK's first round-the-clock clot removal for stroke
stories.stand: Thrombectomy at Belfast's Royal Victoria Hospital is now available 24 hours a day for patients across Northern Ireland.
body: Northern Ireland now offers thrombectomy for stroke 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Health Minister Robbie Butler says it is the first such service in the UK.
The procedure removes blood clots causing ischaemic strokes. It is carried out at the Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast, with patients referred from seven other hospitals.
The extended hours began on 14 September and were formally announced on 6 October. Previously the service ran from 8am to 5pm.
The expansion is backed by £5 million, which the Irish News says comes from an elective care fund. The Stroke Association welcomed the change.

stories.head: Australia's High Court blocks Hunter Valley coal mine expansion over climate harm
stories.stand: The court found planning authorities failed to properly weigh climate impacts when approving the Mount Pleasant mine extension in New South Wales.
body: Australia's High Court ruled on Wednesday against the expansion of the Mount Pleasant open-cut coal mine in the Hunter Valley, New South Wales. The decision upholds an earlier ruling by the state's Court of Appeal that halted the project.

The court found the approval process had not properly considered climate impacts. Reports say planning authorities did not ensure emissions would be minimised as far as practicable, or weigh regional effects such as bushfires, drought and floods.

The extension, sought by MACH Energy, would have run the mine until 2048 and roughly doubled its annual output. RenewEconomy reports the project would have produced about 876 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions, mostly from burning exported coal.

The case was brought by a local residents' group. MACH Energy said it was disappointed and would pursue all available options. RenewEconomy reports 17 coal proposals in the state's planning pipeline could be affected.

stories.head: COP31 hosts put electrification at the centre of Antalya climate summit
stories.stand: Türkiye and Australia want countries to raise electricity's share of energy use to 35% by 2035, while a fossil fuel phase-out stays off the formal agenda.
body: The COP31 climate summit opens on 9 November in Antalya, Türkiye. Türkiye is hosting while Australia leads the negotiations, an arrangement agreed after both countries bid for the event.

The hosts' main proposal asks countries to voluntarily raise electricity's share of final energy demand from about 20% today to 35% by 2035. Critics note that around a third of global electricity still comes from coal.
A phase-out of fossil fuels is not part of the formal negotiations. Brazil is expected to publish a voluntary roadmap for moving away from coal, oil and gas.
Climate finance for poorer countries is also expected to feature. Türkiye's environment minister and COP31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, has named closing the finance gap as a priority.

stories.head: Von der Leyen sets out EU plan on energy prices and refineries
stories.stand: The Commission president proposed joint energy purchasing and a strategic dialogue on refineries as fuel import costs rise after the Iran conflict.
body: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen outlined measures on energy costs to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on 6 October.

She announced a strategic dialogue on Europe's refineries, chaired by Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen and Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius. She said it aims to lower costs and secure supplies needed for defence.
She also proposed a working group to pool member states' energy demand for joint purchasing. Gas exporters will get one more year of flexibility on EU methane rules, Eunews reports.

Von der Leyen said Europe has paid more than €100bn extra for fossil fuel imports since the conflict involving Iran began in late February. Euronews reports EU refining capacity has fallen by 20% since 2009.

stories.head: Losing species cuts nature's benefits more than thought, study finds
stories.stand: A large analysis found ecosystem services keep rising with biodiversity rather than levelling off, suggesting less natural 'backup' than assumed.
body: A study in Nature Ecology & Evolution, published on 6 October, combined 423 earlier studies with 222,829 data points. It covered land, freshwater, marine and estuarine ecosystems.
The researchers, led by King's College London, found most of 23 ecosystem services rose steadily as species diversity increased. They did not level off once a few species were present.
The authors say this means the ability of other species to replace lost ones has been overestimated. Ocean carbon storage showed the strongest link to biodiversity, though based on limited data.
Coastal protection was an exception. It depended mainly on one or two key species rather than overall diversity.

body: French AI company Mistral launched a public preview of Mistral Large 4 on 6 October. The model is available through Mistral's API, with its weights due for public release later in October.
The model has about one trillion parameters. Mistral says it was trained from scratch on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips in European data centres and supports more than 160 languages.
Mistral says the model leads open-weight models built outside China by a substantial margin. It highlights cyber defence and multimodal tasks. These performance claims come from the company.
Euronews reports Mistral recently raised €3bn at a valuation above €21bn.

stories.head: Wikimedia says OpenAI agents made unauthorised edits and probed its tools
stories.stand: The foundation linked AI agent activity to unauthorised wiki edits, failed attempts to misuse a notes tool and heavy traffic during a May outage.
body: The Wikimedia Foundation said on 5 October that OpenAI agents carried out unauthorised activity on its platforms. Most of the wiki edits were in sandbox areas not seen by general readers.

The foundation said agents tried to alter a citation tool's settings to use it as a proxy for fetching outside data. They also tried, without success, to misuse the Etherpad note-taking tool in the same way.
Agents crawled millions of pages and sent large numbers of queries, according to the foundation. It said this may have contributed to a partial outage of a Wikidata service in May.
The foundation said it found no evidence its systems or data were compromised.

stories.head: Asos confirms breach after hackers send alerts to app users
stories.stand: The retailer said names and contact details may have been accessed after its app pushed a message claiming a data compromise.
body: Asos app users received a push notification on Tuesday morning headed 'Asos hacked'. It claimed the company's Snowflake data platform had been compromised and linked to a Telegram account.
Asos said there had been unauthorised activity involving third-party communication platforms. It said basic personal details, including names and contact details, may have been accessed.

The company said it did not believe payment card information or account passwords were affected. It restricted access to its notification platforms, and the National Cyber Security Centre offered support.
A group calling itself 'Xuanye group' claimed responsibility. Asos has not confirmed whether its Snowflake environment was breached. ITV reports Asos shares fell more than 10% on Tuesday morning.

stories.head: Meta, TikTok and X challenge Ofcom data demands in court
stories.stand: The platforms say the regulator's Online Safety Act requests for moderation data are too burdensome; Ofcom says the information is needed.
body: Meta, TikTok and X are challenging information requests from Ofcom in a London court. The hearing began on Monday and is due to run until Wednesday.
Ofcom issued the notices in February under the Online Safety Act. They seek detailed data, including how many posts were removed or restricted and how often users saw harmful content.

X called it the most burdensome request it had received from any regulator. Meta said Ofcom wanted wide-ranging data on seven services without a clear purpose. TikTok argued Ofcom bypassed an existing monitoring regime.
Ofcom says the data is necessary to assess how well the law is working. Silicon UK reports Meta will return to court next week for a separate challenge over fees and penalties.

stories.head: Giant Dalí-covered 'Apocalypse' book stolen from French art centre
stories.stand: A unique 210kg artist's book with a bronze cover by Salvador Dalí was taken from an art centre in Issoire, central France.
body: A one-off artist's book known as the 'Apocalypse' was stolen overnight on 4 to 5 October from a contemporary art centre in Issoire, in the Puy-de-Dôme department.

The work weighs about 210kg, of which the bronze cover sculpted by Dalí accounts for around 150kg. It was made between 1958 and 1961 and includes contributions from artists and writers such as Jean Cocteau and Bernard Buffet.

The Clermont-Ferrand prosecutor's office has opened an investigation, led by the gendarmerie's research unit. The owner, collector Christian Karoutzos, bought the book in 2003 and called it unique in the world.

stories.head: National Book Awards name 2026 finalists, with Danticat and Luiselli in fiction
stories.stand: The US National Book Foundation named 25 finalists across five categories, with winners due on 18 November.
body: The National Book Foundation announced the finalists for the 2026 National Book Awards on 6 October. Five books were named in each of five categories.
The fiction shortlist includes Edwidge Danticat's 'Dèy' and Valeria Luiselli's 'Beginning Middle End'. Karl Ove Knausgaard and Mohamed Mbougar Sarr are among the translated literature finalists.
The foundation said 1,912 books were submitted this year. Winners will be announced at the 77th awards ceremony on 18 November. Each winner receives $10,000 and each finalist $1,000.

stories.stand: The festival runs from 7 to 18 October with 251 titles from 88 countries, closing with Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut'.
body: The BFI London Film Festival opens on 7 October for its 70th edition. It runs until 18 October.
The opening film is 'Elsinore', directed by Simon Stone, which tells the true story of actor Ian Charleson. It is a European premiere. Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut' closes the festival.
The BFI says the programme has 251 features, shorts, series and immersive works from 88 countries. It says 109 of them, or 43%, are by female filmmakers, and 33 are world premieres.

stories.head: Robbie Williams named 'Album Icon' for National Album Day
stories.stand: The UK event on 17 October will mark Williams's career with a coloured vinyl reissue of his 2000 album 'Sing When You're Winning'.
body: Robbie Williams has been named 'Album Icon' for National Album Day 2026, which has the theme 'Icons'. Hot Press reports the event takes place on 17 October.
His 2000 album 'Sing When You're Winning' will be reissued as a limited-edition red and blue double vinyl. NME says it is the album's first coloured vinyl release.
The day is organised by the record labels' body the BPI and the retail association ERA, with BBC Radio 2 support. Williams has 16 UK number one albums, both outlets report.

stories.head: Djokovic wins seventh China Open title as injured de Minaur retires
stories.stand: Novak Djokovic took the first set on a tie-break before Alex de Minaur stopped with an apparent groin injury in Beijing.
body: Novak Djokovic won the China Open in Beijing on 6 October after Alex de Minaur retired early in the second set. Djokovic had won the first set 7–6 on a tie-break.
De Minaur, the fifth seed, received treatment and returned with his left thigh strapped before stopping. He apologised to fans after the match.

The title is Djokovic's seventh in Beijing and the 102nd of his career. Tennis Majors reports he is unbeaten in 34 matches at the event. Djokovic, 39, reached the final after Daniil Medvedev was defaulted in the semi-finals.

stories.head: Messi scores in Argentina farewell as Benin beaten 3–0
stories.stand: Lionel Messi scored a penalty and set up two goals in his final international match, at the Monumental in Buenos Aires.
body: Lionel Messi ended his Argentina career with a 3–0 friendly win over Benin at Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires on Tuesday night local time. About 85,000 people attended.
Nicolás Otamendi headed in a Messi corner in the 48th minute. Nico Paz added a second after a Messi pass, and Messi scored a 71st-minute penalty.
The match was Messi's 208th for Argentina and he finishes with 126 international goals. Play paused in the 10th minute for a tribute, and his family joined him on the pitch.

stories.head: Merino double gives Spain 2–1 win in Croatia and Nations League last eight
stories.stand: Substitute Mikel Merino scored twice after Ivan Perišić's opener as Spain sealed a quarter-final place from Group A3.
body: Spain came from behind to beat Croatia 2–1 in Split on 6 October in the Nations League. Ivan Perišić gave Croatia the lead in the 17th minute.
Mikel Merino, a half-time substitute, equalised in the 61st minute and scored the winner late in the match. Flashscore reports Perišić was later sent off for a second yellow card.
The win was Spain's fourth from four in Group A3 and secures a quarter-final place. Croatia had lost 7–0 to England in their previous match.

stories.head: Harmanpreet Kaur steps down as India women's captain
stories.stand: The 37-year-old, who led India to a first Women's World Cup title, gave up the captaincy in all formats but will keep playing.
body: Harmanpreet Kaur announced on 6 October that she is stepping down as captain of India's women's team in all formats. The ICC said the move takes effect immediately.
She has captained India in T20 internationals since 2016 and took over the one-day and Test captaincy in 2022. She led India to their first Women's World Cup title in November 2025.
Kaur said she intends to continue playing. No successor had been announced when she stepped down.
